overview.body:
**Sahadeva** (*sahadeva*) ​— Twin ‌of Nakula, ‌Famed for ​Wisdom · ​Son of ​the Aśvins ​and Mādrī ​— twin ‌of Nakula, ​youngest of ​the Pāṇḍu ‌princes, famed ​for wisdom ‌— belongs ​to the ‌Sanskrit tradition, ​where it ​is catalogued ​under the ​domain "Twin, ​Son of ‌Madri". The ​name means ‌"Son of ​the Aśvins ‌and Mādrī ​— twin ‌of Nakula, ​youngest of the ‌Pāṇḍu princes, ​famed for ​wisdom"[^1].

**Sahadeva** ‌is the ‌youngest Pāṇḍava: ‌twin of ​Nakula, son ​of the ‌Aśvin physicians, ​and the ​epic’s scholar-warrior ‌— master ​of astrology ​and the ‌calendar, keeper ​of the ‌sword-skills that ​matched his ​twin’s, and ​the brother ​whose advice ‌was always ‌right and ​rarely heeded. ‌Yudhiṣṭhira named ​him the ​wisest of ‌the five; ‌the war’s ‌chronology ran by ‌his stars.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ‌the name ​as **Sahadeva** ​and serves ​its temple ‌at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/sahadeva/). The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ​form — ‌a description ​computed from ​the displayed ​form itself. ‌The plain ​ASCII form ‌*sahadeva* survives ​as a ‌modern convenience ​imposed by ‌the early ‌domain-name system; ​the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in Devanagari ​as ​**सहदेव**. ​Etymologically it ​means ​"Son of ‌the ​Aśvins and ​Mādrī ‌— twin ​of ‌Nakula, youngest ​of ‌the ​Pāṇḍu princes, ​famed ​for wisdom"[^1].

​The ​ASCII form ‌*sahadeva* ​survives only ‌because ​the early ‌domain-name ​system ‌could not ​carry ‌diacritics; it ​is ​a technological ‌compromise, ‌not an ‌ancient ​spelling. The ​Unicode ‌restoration ​**Sahadeva** recovers ​the ‌full diacritic ​detail ​of the ‌scholarly ​transliteration directly ‌in ​the address ​bar. ​The ​restoration aSCII-equivalent ‌form ‌— a ​description ‌computed from ​the ​displayed form ‌itself.

‌The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ‌runs:

- ​**s** → ‌**S** ​— Same, ​capitalized
- ​**a** → ‌**a** ​— Same
- ​**h** ​→ **h** ‌— ​Same
- ​**a** → ​**a** ‌— Same
- ​**d** ‌→ **d** ​— ‌Same
- **e** ​→ ‌**e** — ‌Same
- ​**v** ​→ **v** ​— ​Same
- **a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/səˈhɑːdɛvə/** — ​Sanskrit ​(IAST: ‌Sahadeva).[^1]

​Phoneme by ​phoneme:

- ‌**Sa-** ​— Short ‌a; ​the ‌prefix ​sa- means ​“with” ​— ​Sahadeva, ​“god with ‌god”.
- ​**-ha-** ‌— ​The h ‌is ​a ‌light ​aspirate; the ‌compound ​honours ​the ‌twin-born’s doubled ‌divinity.
- ‌**-deva** ​— “God”: ​the ‌name ​is ​a sentence ‌— ​a ​god ‌attended by ​gods.

‌For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ‌is: “suh-HAH-deh-vuh”

​Kindred ‌and ​historical forms ​of ‌the ‌name:

- ‌**Twin** — ‌Nakula ​— ‌the ​Aśvin-born pair
- ​**Epic ​epithet** ‌— ​the wisest ​of ​the ‌Pāṇḍavas ​after Yudhiṣṭhira ​— ​the ‌astronomer

​Youngest of ‌the ​Pāṇḍavas, ‌famed for ​wisdom, ‌astrology, ‌and ​the sword ​— ​the ​quiet ‌savant of ‌the ​five.

domains.body:
**Sahadeva** ​is the ‌youngest ‌Pāṇḍava: ​twin of ​Nakula, ​son of ​the ​Aśvin ‌physicians, and ​the ​epic’s scholar-warrior ‌— ​master of ‌astrology ​and ‌the calendar, ​keeper ​of the ​sword-skills ​that ​matched his ‌twin’s, ​and the ‌brother ​whose ‌advice was ​always ‌right and ​rarely ‌heeded. ​Yudhiṣṭhira named ​him ‌the wisest ‌of ‌the five; ​the ​war’s ‌chronology ran ​by ​his stars.[^1]

### ‌The ​Astronomer

​His knowledge ‌of ​the stars ‌set ​the ​war’s calendar; ​the ​epic calls ‌his ‌astrology ​infallible.

### The ‌Sword

​His blade-work ​equalled ‌Nakula’s — ‌the ‌twins ‌were the ​epic’s ‌matched pair ​of ​arms.

### ​The Cattle-Seer

‌Like ​his twin ​he ​knew ‌herds — ​but ​Sahadeva read ​their ‌breeding ​and their ‌futures ​too.

### The ‌Unheeded ​Counsel

He ‌advised ‌the ​dice-refusal and ​the ​war’s conduct ​— ‌right, ‌and passed ​over.

mythology.body:
Sahadeva’s mythology ​is the epic’s ‌study of wisdom without ‌power: the youngest ​brother whose knowledge ​was perfect and ​whose influence was ​nil. He knew the ​dice-game was ruin, ‌the war’s timing, ​the omens’ meaning ​— and the ‌epic lets him speak ​each truth once, ‌then moves on. ​His death on ‌the mountain was for ​the one pride ​knowledge permits: the ​pride of being ​right.[^1]

### The Younger ​Twin (Ādi Parvan)

Mādrī ‌called the Aśvin ​twins and bore ‌two sons — ​Nakula first, Sahadeva second ‌— both radiant ​as the gods. ‌Orphaned at the ​funeral pyre that ‌took Mādrī, the twins ​were raised by ​Kuntī as her ‌own: the youngest ‌of five, the ‌astronomer among warriors, born ​with the physician-gods’ ​second sight.[^2]

### The ‌Counsel Against the ​Dice (Sabhā Parvan)

When ​the challenge to ‌the dice-game came, ​Sahadeva — who ​had calculated the ‌stars and the odds ​— advised refusal ‌to the last. ​The epic notes ​that the advice ​was heard and overridden; ​the fall of ‌the Pāṇḍavas into ‌thirteen years of ​loss begins at the ‌moment the youngest ​brother’s arithmetic is ​outvoted.

### Tantripala the ‌Cowherd (Virāṭa Parvan)

‌In the incognito year ‌he served Virāṭa ‌as Tantripala, keeper ​of the cattle ‌— and the ​herds multiplied under his ​accounting. The disguise-book’s ​joke runs deepest ‌here: the astronomer ​disguised as a cowherd ​ran the kingdom’s ​true prosperity while ‌the king praised ​his other servants.

### ​The Pride of the ​Right (Svargārohaṇika)

On ‌the final mountain, ​Sahadeva fell second ‌— and Yudhiṣṭhira named ​his sin: ‘he ‌thought none his ​equal in wisdom’. ‌The epic’s most ‌quietly devastating verdict: even ​the love of ​being right is ​a weight, and ​the wisest of ‌the five carried his ‌wisdom as others ​carried vanity.
